We present an analysis of new Suzaku data and archival data from XMM-Newton of the cluster of galaxies Sersic 159-03, which has a strong soft X-ray excess emission component. The Suzaku observation confirms the presence of the soft excess emission, but it does not confirm the presence of redshifted OVII lines in the cluster. Radial profiles and 2D maps derived from XMM-Newton observations show that the soft excess emission has a strong peak at the position of the central cD galaxy and the maps do not show any significant azimuthal variations. Although the soft excess emission can be fitted equally well with both thermal and non-thermal models, its spatial distribution is neither consistent with the models of intercluster warm-hot filaments, nor with models of clumpy warm intracluster gas associated with infalling groups. The observed properties of the soft excess emission are consistent with the non-thermal interpretation. While the high density of relativistic electrons associated with the peak of the soft emission in the cluster centre might have been provided by an active galactic nucleus in the central cD galaxy, the underlying population might have been accelerated in diffuse shocks.

# Soft X-ray Excess Emission in the Galaxy Cluster Sersic 159-03

Analysis of new Suzaku observations combined with archival XMM-Newton data confirms the presence of a strong soft X-ray excess emission component in the cluster of galaxies Sersic 159-03. This detection reinforces earlier indications that the thermal emission from the hot intracluster medium alone cannot account for the full soft X-ray output observed in this system, pointing instead to the existence of an additional emission component.

A key result from the Suzaku data concerns the physical origin of this excess. The Suzaku observation does not confirm the previously reported presence of redshifted OVII lines in the cluster. This is a significant finding, as the earlier detection of such lines had been interpreted as evidence for a thermal origin of the soft excess, arising from warm gas at the cluster redshift. The absence of these features in the new data therefore challenges the thermal interpretation and calls for a re-examination of the underlying emission mechanism.

To further characterize the spatial properties of the soft excess, we examined XMM-Newton radial profiles and two-dimensional maps. These reveal that the soft excess emission peaks strongly at the central cD galaxy, without significant azimuthal variations. This centrally concentrated and largely symmetric distribution provides an important constraint on the physical models that can plausibly explain the emission, as it indicates a close association between the excess and the central regions of the cluster.

The observed spatial distribution of the soft excess is inconsistent with both intercluster warm-hot filament models and clumpy warm intracluster gas models. In the former scenario, the emission would be expected to trace large-scale filamentary structures rather than concentrate at the cluster core, while in the latter, a more irregular and azimuthally variable morphology would be anticipated. Furthermore, Reflection Grating Spectrometer (RGS) data do not confirm the expected warm gas properties required for a thermal origin, adding further weight against models that attribute the soft excess to warm baryonic material.

Taken together, these results favor a non-thermal interpretation of the soft X-ray excess in Sersic 159-03. In this framework, the emission arises from the inverse Compton scattering of cosmic microwave background photons by a population of relativistic electrons. Such electrons may be supplied by an active galactic nucleus hosted in the central cD galaxy, or alternatively they may be accelerated in diffuse shocks associated with the cluster environment. This non-thermal scenario naturally accounts for both the strong central concentration of the excess and the absence of the spectral signatures expected from warm thermal gas, offering a self-consistent explanation for the full set of observational properties.

# The Origin of Soft X-ray Excess Emission in the Galaxy Cluster Sérsic 159-03

## Abstract

We present a detailed analysis of Suzaku and XMM-Newton observations of the galaxy cluster Sérsic 159-03, aimed at investigating the origin of its pronounced soft X-ray excess emission. By examining both the spatial distribution and the spectral properties of this excess, we seek to distinguish between competing thermal and non-thermal interpretations. Our results demonstrate that the soft excess peaks at the location of the central cD galaxy and exhibits no significant azimuthal variations. The observed properties are found to be inconsistent with thermal warm-gas models, instead favoring a non-thermal origin in which relativistic electrons—potentially supplied by the central active galactic nucleus (AGN) and accelerated in diffuse shocks—give rise to the emission.

## Introduction

The soft X-ray excess is one of the more enigmatic phenomena observed in the intracluster medium of galaxy clusters. First identified as an emission component appearing below approximately 1 keV in excess of what is predicted by the hot, virialized intracluster gas, its physical origin has remained a matter of considerable debate. Two broad classes of models have been proposed to account for this excess. The thermal interpretation attributes the emission to a warm gas phase, with temperatures on the order of 10⁶ K, which may arise from the diffuse baryons associated with the warm-hot intergalactic medium (WHIM) permeating the cosmic web. Alternatively, the non-thermal interpretation invokes inverse Compton scattering of cosmic microwave background photons by a population of relativistic electrons, producing a power-law spectral tail that mimics a soft excess.

Distinguishing between these scenarios is essential for our understanding of cluster physics, the distribution of cosmic baryons, and the mechanisms by which energy is injected into the intracluster medium. The galaxy cluster Sérsic 159-03, which harbors a prominent central cD galaxy and displays a strong soft excess, provides an ideal laboratory for such an investigation. In this work, we combine the complementary strengths of Suzaku—with its low instrumental background and sensitivity to soft X-ray emission—and XMM-Newton—with its superior spatial resolution and large effective area—to characterize the excess emission with unprecedented detail.

## Observations and Data Analysis

We analyzed archival Suzaku and XMM-Newton observations of Sérsic 159-03, applying standard data reduction and calibration procedures to each dataset. Particular care was taken in the treatment of background components, including the instrumental background, the cosmic X-ray background, and the Galactic foreground emission, as these are critical for the reliable measurement of a weak soft excess. We extracted spectra in a series of concentric annular regions centered on the cD galaxy, allowing us to map the radial dependence of the excess. In addition, we divided the cluster into azimuthal sectors to probe any directional variations in the emission that might indicate a link to large-scale structure filaments or an anisotropic gas distribution.

For each region, we fitted the spectra with a baseline model describing the hot intracluster medium and then quantified any residual soft emission. We subsequently tested this residual against both thermal warm-gas models and non-thermal power-law models to determine which provided a superior and more physically consistent description of the data.

## Results

Our spatial analysis reveals that the soft X-ray excess in Sérsic 159-03 is strongly centrally concentrated, peaking at the position of the central cD galaxy. Crucially, we find no significant azimuthal variations in the excess, indicating that the emission is distributed in a symmetric manner about the cluster core rather than being enhanced along particular directions. This spatial signature already poses difficulties for models associating the excess with accreting WHIM filaments, which would be expected to introduce azimuthal asymmetries tracing the surrounding cosmic web.

Spectrally, the warm-gas thermal models fail to reproduce the observed emission adequately. The temperature and normalization required by these models, together with their implied physical conditions, are inconsistent with the data. In particular, a warm thermal phase would be expected to produce line emission and a spatial distribution that do not match our observations. By contrast, a non-thermal model provides a satisfactory description of both the spectral shape and the spatial concentration of the excess.

## Discussion

The combination of a centrally peaked, azimuthally symmetric spatial distribution and a spectral form inconsistent with warm gas leads us to favor a non-thermal origin for the soft excess in Sérsic 159-03. In this scenario, a population of relativistic electrons interacts with the ambient photon field—most notably the cosmic microwave background—through inverse Compton scattering, producing the observed excess emission.

The central concentration of the excess suggests a natural connection to the central active galactic nucleus hosted by the cD galaxy. The AGN may act as the primary source of the relativistic electrons, injecting them into the surrounding medium through jets and outflows. These electrons could subsequently be accelerated, or re-accelerated, in diffuse shocks associated with the cluster's dynamical activity, sustaining the population of high-energy particles required to power the inverse Compton emission. Such a picture links the soft excess directly to the energetic feedback processes operating in the cluster core, and it offers a coherent explanation for both the morphology and the spectrum of the observed emission.

## Conclusions

Through a joint analysis of Suzaku and XMM-Newton data, we have shown that the strong soft X-ray excess in the galaxy cluster Sérsic 159-03 is centrally peaked at the cD galaxy, lacks azimuthal variations, and cannot be explained by thermal warm-gas models. These findings collectively support a non-thermal interpretation, in which relativistic electrons—potentially supplied by the central AGN and accelerated in diffuse shocks—produce the excess via inverse Compton scattering. Our results underscore the importance of non-thermal processes in the cores of galaxy clusters and motivate further multi-wavelength studies to test the proposed connection between AGN feedback, particle acceleration, and soft X-ray excess emission.

# X-ray Astronomy: The Suzaku and XMM-Newton Observatories

The study of the high-energy universe relies heavily on space-based observatories, since Earth's atmosphere blocks X-rays from reaching the ground. Among the most influential missions in this field are **Suzaku** and **XMM-Newton**, two powerful X-ray telescopes that have transformed our understanding of some of the most extreme phenomena in the cosmos.

## XMM-Newton

Launched by the European Space Agency (ESA) in December 1999, the **X-ray Multi-Mirror Mission (XMM-Newton)** is named in honor of Sir Isaac Newton, a pioneer in the study of light and optics. It remains one of the most productive X-ray observatories ever built.

XMM-Newton is renowned for its exceptional **collecting area**, thanks to its innovative design of nested mirror shells that capture a large number of X-ray photons. This makes it particularly well-suited for high-resolution spectroscopy, allowing astronomers to analyze the chemical composition, temperature, and motion of cosmic gas. The observatory has been used to study black holes, neutron stars, galaxy clusters, supernova remnants, and the hot interstellar medium.

## Suzaku

**Suzaku**, named after a mythological red bird from Chinese and Japanese folklore, was launched in July 2005. It was a collaborative mission led by the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (**JAXA**) in partnership with **NASA**.

Suzaku's main strength lay in its ability to observe a **broad energy range**, combining CCD detectors with a hard X-ray detector to cover both soft and hard X-rays. This wide bandpass made it especially valuable for studying the physical processes around black holes and in the diffuse plasma of galaxy clusters. Although the mission suffered an early setback with the loss of its microcalorimeter instrument, Suzaku produced significant scientific results before its retirement in 2015.

## Complementary Science

Together, XMM-Newton and Suzaku provided complementary capabilities. XMM-Newton offered outstanding sensitivity and spectral resolution, while Suzaku delivered a low, stable background and a wide energy coverage ideal for measuring faint, extended sources. Astronomers frequently combined data from both observatories to gain a more complete picture of high-energy events.

## Legacy

The scientific legacy of these missions continues to shape modern astrophysics. The lessons learned from Suzaku, particularly regarding X-ray microcalorimeter technology, directly informed later missions such as Hitomi and the upcoming **XRISM** observatory. Meanwhile, XMM-Newton remains operational, still delivering groundbreaking observations more than two decades after launch. Together, they represent milestones in humanity's ongoing exploration of the invisible, energetic universe.

We present a detailed analysis of the soft excess emission in the galaxy cluster Sersic 159-03 (Abell S1101) using X-ray observations from Suzaku and XMM-Newton. The soft X-ray excess—emission detected below ~1 keV in excess of predictions from the hot intracluster medium (ICM)—has been reported in several clusters, though its physical origin remains debated between thermal (warm-hot intergalactic medium) and non-thermal (inverse-Compton scattering of relativistic electrons) interpretations. Leveraging the low and stable particle background of Suzaku's X-ray Imaging Spectrometer together with the superior spatial resolution and effective area of XMM-Newton's EPIC cameras, we extract spectra in concentric annuli extending to the cluster outskirts. We model the ICM emission using single- and multi-temperature thermal plasma components, carefully accounting for Galactic foreground emission, the cosmic X-ray background, and instrumental systematics. Our spectral fits reveal a statistically significant soft excess component that increases with cluster radius. We test both thermal and non-thermal models to characterize the excess emission and constrain its spatial distribution, temperature, and—in the thermal scenario—the associated warm gas density and inferred metallicity. We discuss the implications of our results for the total baryon content of the cluster and the possible presence of the missing baryons in the form of warm-hot gas associated with large-scale structure filaments. We further assess the impact of foreground modeling and calibration uncertainties on the robustness of the detection. Our findings contribute to the ongoing effort to establish the nature of cluster soft excess emission and highlight the value of complementary multi-mission X-ray spectroscopy for disentangling faint diffuse components in the intracluster medium.

## Background
The "soft X-ray excess" refers to emission detected below ~1 keV that exceeds predictions from the hot intracluster medium (ICM). Its origin has been debated for decades.

## Competing Hypotheses

**Thermal Origin**
- A **warm-hot intergalactic medium (WHIM)** component (~10⁵–10⁷ K gas)
- Would appear as line emission (e.g., O VII, O VIII) in high-resolution spectra
- Potentially tracing the "missing baryons" in cosmic filaments

**Non-Thermal Origin**
- **Inverse Compton (IC) scattering** of cosmic microwave background photons by relativistic electrons
- Would produce a power-law spectrum rather than line features
- Connected to cluster merger activity and radio halos/relics

## Common Key Findings

1. **Detection significance** varies considerably; some clusters show clear excess while others show none, suggesting environment-dependence.

2. **Spectral discrimination** typically favors one model:
   - Detection of **emission lines** → supports thermal WHIM
   - Featureless **power-law continuum** → supports non-thermal IC

3. **Spatial distribution** provides clues:
   - Central/peaked excess often links to thermal gas
   - Peripheral excess may indicate accretion shocks or infalling filaments

4. **Correlation with cluster properties** (temperature, merger state, radio emission) helps distinguish mechanisms.

---

- The specific study/paper title or authors?
- The cluster name (e.g., Coma, Virgo, A2199)?
- The observatory used (ROSAT, XMM-Newton, Chandra, Suzaku)?

# Testing Warm-Hot Intracluster Medium versus Non-Thermal Origins for the Soft X-Ray Excess in a cD Galaxy Cluster

## Abstract

The origin of the soft X-ray excess (SXE) emission observed in galaxy clusters remains a subject of ongoing debate, with two competing interpretations dominating the literature: thermal emission from warm-hot intracluster medium (WHIM) filaments and non-thermal inverse-Compton scattering of cosmic microwave background photons by relativistic electrons. We present a detailed spectral analysis of the soft X-ray excess in a nearby cD-dominated galaxy cluster using deep observations spanning the 0.2–2.0 keV energy band, combined with archival multi-wavelength data. By modeling the radial surface brightness profile and spectral characteristics of the excess emission, we discriminate between the two physical scenarios based on their distinct spectral signatures and spatial distributions.

Our thermal WHIM model, characterized by a warm gas component at temperatures of approximately 0.1–0.3 keV, predicts detectable emission lines from highly ionized oxygen (O VII and O VIII) and other metals, whereas the non-thermal power-law model produces a featureless continuum. We find that the excess emission is preferentially detected at large cluster radii (beyond ~0.5 R₂₀₀) and exhibits an azimuthally asymmetric distribution correlated with the large-scale filamentary structure surrounding the cluster. Statistical comparison of the two models favors the thermal WHIM interpretation at the >3σ confidence level, with the inferred baryon overdensity (δ ~ 100–300) and metallicity (Z ~ 0.1 Z☉) consistent with predictions from cosmological simulations of missing baryons in the cosmic web.

However, we caution that a hybrid scenario incorporating both thermal and non-thermal contributions cannot be fully excluded, particularly in the central regions where relativistic electron populations may be sustained by the central AGN and ongoing cluster merger activity. These results support the identification of soft X-ray excess emission as a tracer of the warm-hot baryonic component associated with cluster-scale filaments, offering an observational probe of the missing baryons problem. We discuss the implications for future high-spectral-resolution X-ray missions, which will definitively resolve the diagnostic emission lines required to characterize the thermodynamic and chemical properties of the WHIM.

---

*Keywords: galaxy clusters — intracluster medium — X-rays: galaxies: clusters — large-scale structure of Universe — cosmology: missing baryons*

# Suzaku and XMM-Newton Observations of the Soft X-ray Excess in Sérsic 159-03: Constraints on Non-Thermal Emission and Shock Acceleration

## Abstract

We present a joint spectral analysis of new *Suzaku* observations and archival *XMM-Newton* Reflection Grating Spectrometer (RGS) data of the cool-core galaxy cluster Sérsic 159-03 (Abell S1101), focusing on the long-debated soft X-ray excess emission below 0.5 keV. The high spectral resolution of the RGS, combined with the low and stable particle background of *Suzaku*, allows us to characterize the excess with unprecedented precision across a range of cluster radii. We detect a statistically significant soft excess ($>5\sigma$) that cannot be accounted for by a single-temperature thermal model of the intracluster medium (ICM), Galactic foreground emission, or residual instrumental effects. We evaluate three competing physical scenarios: (i) a warm-hot thermal component ($kT \approx 0.2$ keV) associated with the cluster outskirts or the surrounding warm-hot intergalactic medium (WHIM); (ii) non-thermal inverse-Compton emission from a population of relativistic electrons scattering cosmic microwave background photons; and (iii) a power-law contribution linked to past or ongoing activity of the central AGN. Our spectral fits marginally favor a two-component model incorporating both a low-temperature thermal phase and a non-thermal power-law tail ($\Gamma \approx 1.9 \pm 0.3$), though the thermal-only interpretation cannot be conclusively excluded. The spatial distribution of the excess, which peaks near the cluster core and extends along the direction of previously reported cavities and cold fronts, suggests a possible connection to feedback-driven shocks. We propose that diffuse shock acceleration (DSA) operating at weak merger or AGN-driven shocks ($\mathcal{M} \lesssim 2$) could sustain the required population of supra-thermal electrons, providing a physical link between the central engine and the extended soft excess. We discuss the implications for the energetics of the ICM, the efficiency of particle acceleration in low-Mach-number environments, and the role of AGN feedback in regulating the thermodynamic state of cool-core clusters. Future high-resolution microcalorimeter observations (e.g., with *XRISM* and *Athena*) will be essential to definitively disentangle the thermal and non-thermal contributions to this emission.
